items.title: [Bug]: [Hermes Desktop]: desktop.log / System "RECENT LOGS" have no timestamps

labels.name: sweeper:risk-platform-windows
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may break or behave differently on native Windows

items.body:
### Bug Description

The Desktop app's log surface — both `desktop.log` (`<HERMES_HOME>/logs/desktop.log`)
and the GUI "System → RECENT LOGS" view — contains lines without any timestamp:
```
[hermes] [boot] Resolving Hermes backend
[hermes] [boot] Resolving Hermes runtime
[hermes] Hermes backend exited (0)
[hermes] [boot] Hermes backend exited before it became ready (0).
```
Meanwhile `gateway.log` and `agent.log` (Python logging) include full timestamps:
```
2026-07-12 16:22:17,540 INFO gateway.run: Starting Hermes Gateway...
2026-08-10 04:10:38,423 INFO hermes_cli.plugins: Plugin 'web-brave-free' ...


### Steps to Reproduce

1. Open Hermes Desktop on Windows.
2. Open System → RECENT LOGS (or read `<HERMES_HOME>/logs/desktop.log`).
3. Observe: every line starts with `[hermes] ` but has no date/time.


### Expected Behavior

Each desktop log line should carry a timestamp (like the Python logs do), e.g.
`[2026-08-12T08:03:31.123Z] [hermes] [boot] Resolving Hermes backend`.


### Actual Behavior

Lines have only the `[hermes] ` prefix, no timestamp.

### Affected Component

Other

### Messaging Platform (if gateway-related)

N/A (CLI only)

### Debug Report

```shell
NOTE: `hermes debug share` intentionally NOT run — logs contain secrets/tokens.
Not required for this report: it is a pure code-level gap with a one-line fix.
A redacted `desktop.log` excerpt is shown in "Additional Logs" below.
```

### Operating System

Windows 10

### Python Version

3.11.15

### Hermes Version

0.20.0 (HEAD 76d832d38)

### Additional Logs / Traceback (optional)

```shell
`<HERMES_HOME>/logs/desktop.log` — first lines (redacted, no timestamps present):

[hermes] [boot] Resolving Hermes backend
[hermes] [boot] Resolving Hermes runtime
[hermes] [boot] Hermes runtime is ready
[hermes] [backend] `serve` supported for Hermes at C:\Users\Branwyn\AppData\Local\hermes\hermes-agent (venv: ...)
[hermes] [boot] Starting Hermes backend via Hermes at ...
[hermes] Hermes backend exited (0)
[hermes] [boot] Hermes backend exited before it became ready (0).
```

### Root Cause Analysis (optional)

`apps/desktop/electron/main.ts` — `rememberLog(chunk)` (line 1266):
```ts
function rememberLog(chunk) {
  const text = String(chunk || '').trim()
  if (!text) return
  const lines = text.split(/\r?\n/).map(line => `[hermes] ${line}`)
  hermesLog.push(...lines)
  desktopLogBuffer += `${lines.join('\n')}\n`
  ...
}
```
Only a `[hermes] ` prefix is prepended; no `new Date()` is added. The same
buffer feeds both the on-disk file and the GUI "RECENT LOGS" view, so both
surfaces lack timestamps.


### Proposed Fix (optional)

```ts
const lines = text.split(/\r?\n/).map(line => `[${new Date().toISOString()}] [hermes] ${line}`)
```
One line. Desktop log lines then carry an ISO timestamp identical in spirit to
the Python logs (`2026-07-12 16:22:17,540`).


### Are you willing to submit a PR for this?

- [ ] I'd like to fix this myself and submit a PR

items.title: [Bug]: post-compression Desktop session replays an earlier user prompt as a fresh turn

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

labels.name: P1
labels.description: High — major feature broken, no workaround

labels.name: sweeper:risk-session-state
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may lose/corrupt/mis-associate session or context state

items.body:
## Summary

In a long-running Hermes Desktop session that had already rotated through context compression, Hermes replayed an earlier real user prompt as a fresh turn after a newer user turn had completed.

The user did not resend the earlier prompt. This was not only a duplicated chat bubble: `state.db` contains two separate active `role=user` rows with identical content, and `agent.log` shows the agent loop starting the same prompt twice.

This is a current-main regression in the same safety class as closed #14521 / PR #20169, but the observed path is different: the duplicated prompt is a recent real user turn in a compressed Desktop session, not an old fallback-summary fragment.

## Environment

- Hermes Agent: `v0.20.0 (2026.8.3)`
- Source checkout: `76d832d38`
- Surface: Hermes Desktop
- OS: macOS 26.6.1
- Model/provider: `gpt-5.6-sol` via `openai-codex`
- Compression mode: automatic rotation compression
- Busy-input mode: `interrupt`

## Observed timeline

Session IDs and prompt text below are sanitized; timestamps are local.

1. `16:23:19` — compression completed successfully and rotated the session (`split_status=rotated_committed`).
2. `16:30:57.258` — the agent loop accepted user prompt **P**:

   ```text
   conversation turn ... msg='deepseek ... released a new flash model ... I changed all settings to flash'
   ```

3. A different, newer user question was then handled, and its assistant reply completed at `16:31:57.211`.
4. `16:31:57.257` — immediately after that reply completed, the agent loop started another turn with the old prompt **P** again:

   ```text
   conversation turn ... msg='deepseek ... released a new flash model ... I changed all settings to flash'
   ```

5. `16:31:57.259` — preflight compression fired for this replayed turn:

   ```text
   Preflight compression: ~252,025 tokens >= 231,200 threshold
   context compression started: ... messages=145
   ```

There was no user resend between steps 3 and 4.

## Durable database evidence

Read-only inspection of `~/.hermes/state.db` found two separate active rows in the same session with byte-identical user content:

```text
id=68566 role=user active=1 compacted=0 timestamp=16:30:57.263 content=P
id=68578 role=user active=1 compacted=0 timestamp=16:33:19.463 content=P
```

A different legitimate user message and assistant response occur between these rows. The second row is therefore not the same durable row merely rendered twice.

The later database timestamp appears to be the eventual flush time; the agent log proves the second execution began at `16:31:57.257`.

## Expected behavior

- A real user message is accepted exactly once unless the user explicitly uses retry/resend.
- Context compression, session rotation, interruption, and reconciliation must never promote a prior user turn back into the inbound queue.
- If a turn is interrupted by a newer user message, the old prompt may remain historical context, but it must not automatically start again after the newer turn completes.

## Actual behavior

- Hermes persisted the same user prompt twice.
- The agent loop executed it twice.
- In a previous occurrence, the agent explicitly asked the user to stop repeatedly sending the same message even though the user had submitted it only once. The exact repetition count mentioned by the agent was not recovered and is not treated as verified.

## Impact

This can repeat non-idempotent instructions and tool side effects without user intent. It also misattributes the replay to the user, derails the current task, and inflates context/token use.

## Reproduction pattern

The issue is timing/state dependent rather than a deterministic short-session repro:

1. Use a long Hermes Desktop session until automatic compression rotates it.
2. Submit a user prompt while the session is large.
3. While that turn is active, submit a different newer message with busy-input mode set to `interrupt`.
4. Allow the newer message's assistant reply to finish.
5. Observe whether the earlier prompt is started again automatically.
6. Verify both `agent.log` (`conversation turn`) and `state.db` (`messages.role='user'`).

## Related issues and exclusions

- **#14521**: closest historical bug class, closed after #20169; this report reproduces real-user-turn reinjection on current main.
- **#68979 / #69682** and **#83154**: Desktop optimistic-bubble ordering/rendering. This report is not renderer-only because duplicate durable rows and duplicate agent turns are present.
- **#75145**: duplicate transcript replay diagnostics; broader feature request, not this concrete unintended inbound-turn execution.
- **#79278**: dropped tool results causing side-effect retries; related safety impact, but no missing tool result is required here.

## Suggested regression test

Create a rotated/compressed Desktop session, start user prompt P, interrupt it with newer prompt Q, complete Q, then assert:

1. P appears only once among durable user-originated rows;
2. the agent loop does not start P again after Q completes;
3. a subsequent preflight compression does not re-anchor or restore P as the current turn;
4. resume/hydration preserves the same invariant.

items.title: [Bug]: Whitespace after `/` is treated as an empty prefix and suggests every slash command

labels.name: comp/cli
labels.description: CLI entry point, hermes_cli/, setup wizard

items.body:
## Bug description

In the classic CLI, inserting whitespace immediately after the leading slash turns an intended command such as:

```text
/ btw patch what means
```

into an empty slash-command prefix. Hermes then prints `Ambiguous command` followed by essentially every registered command.

This is both noisy and misleading: the user made one local syntax error, but the CLI presents the entire command/skill inventory as possible matches.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Start the classic CLI with `hermes`.
2. Enter:

   ```text
   / btw patch what means
   ```

3. Observe a very long `Did you mean:` list containing nearly all slash commands and installed skill commands.

A bare `/` reaches the same empty-prefix class.

## Expected behavior

Hermes should reject the malformed slash syntax with one focused message, for example:

```text
Invalid slash command syntax: remove the space after `/`.
Did you mean: /btw patch what means?
```

It should not execute the corrected command automatically, because automatic normalization could turn a typo such as `/ clear` or `/ exit --delete` into an unintended side effect.

For a bare `/`, Hermes should point to `/help` without enumerating every command as a match.

## Actual behavior

The CLI reports the input as ambiguous and suggests all commands.

## Root cause on current `main`

At `main` commit `a5170af4a87d`:

- `cli.py::_looks_like_slash_command()` accepts `/ btw ...` because the first whitespace-delimited word is the bare `/` and therefore contains no additional slash.
- `HermesCLI.process_command()` resolves `cmd_lower.split()[0].lstrip("/")` to an empty command name.
- The fallback prefix matcher then uses `typed_base == "/"`; all built-in/skill command keys begin with `/`, so every entry satisfies `c.startswith(typed_base)`.

## Suggested regression coverage

- `/ btw explain patch` produces one focused syntax hint containing `/btw explain patch` and does not dispatch `/background`.
- bare `/` points to `/help` and does not emit the full command list.
- normal prefixes such as `/con` retain existing unique-prefix behavior.

## Environment

- Hermes Agent: current `main` at `a5170af4a87d`
- Surface: classic CLI
- OS: Linux

items.title: [Bug]: Background-review cancellation is fire-and-forget, allowing a residual same-session turn race

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

labels.name: P1

labels.description: Sweeper risk: may lose/corrupt/mis-associate session or context state

items.body:
## Bug description

The fix merged in #82418 cancels an in-flight background memory/skill review when the next live turn starts, but the cancellation is explicitly fire-and-forget. The live turn immediately continues into turn setup, preflight compression, Relay instrumentation, and the provider call before the review has acknowledged that it stopped.

As a result, current `main` can still run two Hermes turns concurrently under the same parent `session_id` for a short but correctness-relevant window.

This is a residual race after #82418, not a duplicate of the original report: registration and cancellation now work, but there is no cancellation-completion handoff.

## Production evidence

A real long-running CLI session on 2026-08-12 already contained the #82418 code. The relevant, redacted sequence was:

```text
16:22:05.422 conversation turn: session=<same-session> ... msg='Review the conversation above and update the skill library...'
16:22:05.764 WARNING Skipping Relay instrumentation for concurrent Hermes turn ... in session <same-session>
16:22:05.787 conversation turn: session=<same-session> ... msg='[IMPORTANT: Background process ... completed normally ...]'
16:22:05.823 Preflight compression: ~645,525 tokens >= 217,600 threshold (ctx 272,000)
16:22:05.882 OpenAI client aborted (interrupt_abort, ...) thread=bg-review
16:22:05.883 Turn ended: reason=interrupted_during_api_call ... thread=bg-review
```

The decisive ordering is that the new live turn entered the same session before the background review finished interrupting. The explicit concurrent-turn warning appears before the review exits.

The oversized transcript then required compression from about 645,525 estimated tokens to about 75,544; that compression took about 179 seconds. The report does not claim the short overlap alone created every token in that large session, but it defeats the invariant #82418 intended to restore and compounds accounting/compression behavior on already-long sessions.

## Steps to reproduce deterministically

1. Use a parent agent with `_background_review_agent` pointing to a fake review agent.
2. Make the fake review's `interrupt()` return immediately while a controlled "provider request active" event remains set.
3. Start `run_conversation()` for the next live turn.
4. Observe that current code proceeds into `build_turn_context()` / the live request while the review-active event is still set.

The same race can be reproduced end-to-end by pausing a background review inside its provider call and starting the next live turn.

## Expected behavior

Before a new live turn enters any same-session turn/API/compression path, a prior background review must either:

- acknowledge that its `run_conversation()` request phase has exited, or
- have been prevented from entering that phase by a cancellation generation/token established before the review thread starts.

The foreground turn should retain priority and should not wait indefinitely on non-critical review work.

## Actual behavior

At `main` commit `a5170af4a87d`, `agent/conversation_loop.py` calls:

```python
_pending_review.interrupt("superseded by a new live turn")
```

and immediately continues. The adjacent comment explicitly describes this as fire-and-forget. `agent/background_review.py` only clears `_background_review_agent` after the review's `run_conversation()` returns, but the foreground never waits for or observes that completion.

There is also a startup TOCTOU window: the parent pointer is installed only after the review thread constructs/configures its fork, so a new live turn can check `None` before the review registers and then race a later review start.

## Suggested regression coverage

- A live turn cannot cross into its turn-context/provider boundary while a cancelled review still reports its request phase active.
- A live turn that begins during review-thread startup prevents that review from making its first provider call.
- Review cancellation remains bounded and does not deadlock if the provider abort path is slow.

## Environment

- Hermes Agent: behavior confirmed against current `main` at `a5170af4a87d`
- Surface: classic CLI
- Provider/runtime in observed incident: `openai-codex`
- OS: Linux

## Related

- #82418 — merged initial cancellation fix
- #82070 — superseded original PR

这两个是在服务端硬编码的：`webui/dist/server/index.js` 中有 `function fIe(I){return I==="claude-code"||I==="codex"}`，`/api/coding-agents` 接口也仅返回这两条记录（`{id:"claude-code", name:"Claude Code", provider:"Anthropic", command:"claude"}`、`{id:"codex", name:"Codex", provider:"OpenAI", command:"codex"}`）。

而 OpenCode（https://opencode.ai）是一个热门的开源 AI 编程代理 CLI，Hermes **其实已经部分支持它**：

1. 已有内置 `opencode` 技能（`autonomous-ai-agents/opencode`），可以把编码任务委托给 OpenCode CLI —— 说明 CLI 集成路径已经存在。
2. Hermes 已经内置了 OpenCode Zen / OpenCode Go 作为**模型提供商**（`opencode-zen`、`opencode-go`，`base_url: https://opencode.ai/zen/v1` 和 `/zen/go/v1`）。
3. 像我这类的用户已经安装了 `opencode` CLI（scoop 安装 v1.18.x），**却无法从 Studio 的 Coding Agents 面板启动它** —— UI 上只有 Claude Code 和 Codex 可选。

这里存在不一致：OpenCode 被当作一等公民的*模型提供商*，也有对应的*技能*，但在桌面 UI 里却缺少作为一等公民*编程代理*的入口。

## 建议方案

把 `opencode` 添加为 Hermes Studio Desktop 的第三个编程代理，参照 `claude-code` 和 `codex` 的注册方式：

```js
{id:"opencode", name:"OpenCode", provider:"OpenCode（开源）", command:"opencode", ...}
```

具体来说：

1. **注册到编程代理注册表**（也就是目前只有 `claude-code` 和 `codex` 的那个列表），让它在 Studio 的 Coding Agents 面板中出现，并配上专属图标（`/coding-agents/opencode.svg`）。
2. **启动流程**：后台运行使用 `opencode run <task>`（非交互模式），与现有代理的 launch/native + prepare 接口保持一致。OpenCode 通过 `opencode run "task"` 支持非交互执行，`--model` / 提供商覆盖可以复用已经配置好的 OpenCode Zen/Go 提供商。
3. **配置文件**：支持 `opencode.json` / `.opencode/` 项目配置发现，参照 `claude-code` 处理 `CLAUDE.md`、codex 处理自身配置的方式。
4. **运行与监控**：接入现有的 `/api/coding-agents/:id/runs` + node-pty 隐藏终端机制，让运行记录出现在与 Claude Code/Codex 相同的 UI 中。

内置的 `opencode` 技能（`Delegate coding to OpenCode CLI`）已经掌握了正确的 CLI 调用方式，可以作为实现参考。

## 备选方案

- **仅技能**：`opencode` 技能已经存在，但它只是聊天内的文本委托路径 —— 无法提供 Studio 面板体验（专门的运行 UI、原生会话跟踪、diff 视图、审批流程），而 Claude Code 和 Codex 都有这些。想要一致体验的用户必须能从同一个面板启动 OpenCode。
- **MCP 桥接**：技术上可行，但 coding-agents 面板是已经确立的统一交互入口；另外引入 MCP 会割裂体验。

- [ ] 开发体验（Developer experience，测试、文档、CI）

- [ ] 小（单文件，< 50 行）
- [x] 中（少量文件，< 300 行）
- [ ] 大（新模块或重大重构）

- [ ] 我希望自己实现并提交 PR

items.title: [Bug][Windows] Locale-sensitive timestamp conversion overflows Int32 in Desktop updater

labels.name: sweeper:risk-compatibility
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may break existing users, config, migrations, defaults, or upgrades

labels.name: sweeper:risk-platform-windows
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may break or behave differently on native Windows

items.body:
## Bug Description

On Windows 11, the detached Desktop update hand-off can fail to write its update marker when the system culture uses a comma decimal separator, such as `es-ES`.

The updater logs:

```text
WARNING: could not write update marker: Cannot convert the value "178653613432138" to type "System.Int32". Error: "Value was either too large or too small for an Int32."
```

The warning is non-fatal, but it means the update-in-progress marker is not written during that part of the hand-off. It also causes the update result timestamp to use the same unsafe conversion.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Use Windows 11 with the system culture set to `es-ES` (or another culture where `%s` output uses a comma decimal separator).
2. Run a Desktop update that invokes `scripts/desktop-update/windows.ps1`.
3. Observe the PowerShell hand-off output or `logs/desktop-update-handoff.log`.

The underlying conversion can be reproduced with Windows PowerShell:

```powershell
$s = Get-Date -UFormat %s
[double]::Parse($s, [System.Globalization.CultureInfo]::InvariantCulture)
[int][double]::Parse($s, [System.Globalization.CultureInfo]::InvariantCulture)
```

With `es-ES`, `%s` can produce a value such as `1786536607,39409`. Parsing it with `InvariantCulture` produces `178653660739409`, which overflows `System.Int32`.

## Expected Behavior

The Windows updater should write the update marker and completion result timestamp as Unix seconds without depending on the system locale or converting through `System.Int32`.

## Actual Behavior

The timestamp conversion throws an overflow exception. The exception is caught and logged as a warning, so the hand-off continues without reliably writing the marker:

```text
WARNING: could not write update marker: ... too large or too small for Int32
```

The same conversion is also used for `finished_at` in the update result file.

## Affected Component

- Setup / Installation
- Desktop update hand-off

## Platform

- Windows 11 25H2
- System culture: `es-ES`
- Hermes Agent: v0.20.0 (2026.8.3), git install tracking `main`
- Python: 3.11.15

## Root Cause Analysis

`scripts/desktop-update/windows.ps1` currently uses the following pattern in two places:

```powershell
[int][double]::Parse((Get-Date -UFormat %s), [System.Globalization.CultureInfo]::InvariantCulture)
```

`Get-Date -UFormat %s` is locale-sensitive. Under `es-ES`, its fractional output uses a comma. Parsing that string using `InvariantCulture` treats the comma as a thousands separator rather than a decimal separator, producing a value that exceeds the `Int32` range.

## Proposed Fix

Use the .NET Unix timestamp API directly in both locations:

```powershell
[DateTimeOffset]::UtcNow.ToUnixTimeSeconds()
```

This returns a locale-independent `Int64` Unix timestamp and matches the marker contract consumed by the Desktop and updater code.

A focused source-level regression test can verify that both timestamp writes use this expression and that the unsafe conversion is absent. The fix has been reproduced and verified locally with PowerShell syntax parsing and the `es-ES` failure case.

## Debug Report

No debug report was uploaded because the issue is fully reproducible from the locale, exact log message, source location, and minimal PowerShell reproduction above. No credentials or private logs are needed to diagnose this source-level bug.

labels.name: sweeper:risk-message-delivery
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may drop, duplicate, misroute, or suppress messages

items.body:
## Bug Description
Hermes gateway enters a restart loop (respawn storm) with exit code 75 (GATEWAY_SERVICE_RESTART_EXIT_CODE).

## Root Cause
During gateway shutdown, the cron_provider.stop() call triggers SystemExit(75) which tells systemd to immediately restart the gateway, creating an infinite cycle: start → SIGTERM shutdown → exit 75 → systemd restart → repeat.

## Symptoms
- Gateway repeatedly starts and immediately exits with code 75
- Systemd Restart=on-failure keeps reviving the gateway
- Logs show repeated 'Starting Hermes Gateway...' entries
- Shutdown diagnostics show SystemExit: 75 at cron_provider.stop()

## Environment
- Hermes Agent version: latest
- OS: Linux (Ubuntu/Debian based)
- Running as systemd user service

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Run hermes gateway start
2. Send SIGTERM or use hermes gateway stop
3. Observe gateway exits with code 75 instead of 0
4. Systemd immediately restarts the gateway
5. Loop continues indefinitely

## Expected Fix
gateway shutdown should exit cleanly (code 0) during planned stops, or exit with GATEWAY_FATAL_CONFIG_EXIT_CODE (78) for fatal config errors — not exit 75 which triggers service restart.

## Additional Context
This occurred after a hard-reset of the local server. The gateway was running then became stuck in a restart loop.

items.title: [Bug] Plugin platforms can't enter cron delivery whitelist (_KNOWN_DELIVERY_PLATFORMS is hardcoded, no plugin registration)

labels.name: sweeper:risk-message-delivery
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may drop, duplicate, misroute, or suppress messages

items.body:
### Summary

Plugin platform names (e.g. `napcat`, a OneBot/NapCat QQ adapter for Hermes) **cannot enter the cron delivery whitelist** `_KNOWN_DELIVERY_PLATFORMS` in `cron/scheduler.py` unless the core source is patched locally. The whitelist is a hardcoded `frozenset` of built-in platform names with **no registration mechanism for plugins**, so any cron job with `deliver=napcat:xxx` (or any plugin platform) is rejected by preflight validation.

### Impact

- Cron jobs targeting plugin platforms fail with `blocked_config` at preflight and never run (agent turn is skipped, not just delivery).
- In our install (QQ via the `napcat` platform plugin), every cron job using `deliver=napcat:493505110` — email checks, VPS health patrol, auto-backup, update check, PR watch — was silently blocked until we manually patched the whitelist.
- Any future plugin platform (Mattermost, custom adapters, etc.) hits the same wall: the platform works fine for send_message/home delivery, but cron delivery preflight rejects it.

### Affected code

- `cron/scheduler.py:257` — `_KNOWN_DELIVERY_PLATFORMS = frozenset({...})` hardcoded built-ins.
- `cron/scheduler.py:1167` — preflight `if name in _KNOWN_DELIVERY_PLATFORMS:` rejects unknown platform names (the "check first" path documented at line 1162).

### Related issues (same family)

- #59988 — core platform `whatsapp_cloud` missing from the same whitelist (still OPEN, P2). Shows the whitelist is error-prone: every platform addition is a manual edit that can be forgotten.
- #13707 — resolver/whitelist schema mismatch for `webhook`; fixed on main by switching to `Platform(platform_name.lower())` enum conversion, but the *enum* is core-only and still cannot represent plugin platforms.

### Suggested direction

Give plugin platforms a way to declare cron-delivery capability at registration time, so preflight can compute an effective whitelist = built-ins ∪ registered plugin platforms. For example:

- A registered platform entry (plugin `plugin.yaml` / `PlatformEntry`) could declare `cron_delivery=True` (or derive it from the plugin's adapter implementing the standalone-send interface used by `_deliver_result`).
- Preflight then checks `name in _KNOWN_DELIVERY_PLATFORMS or name in <registered plugin platforms>`, removing the need to hardcode plugin names in core and enabling `deliver=<plugin>:xxx` out of the box.

Happy to provide the patch we're currently running (a local edit adding `"napcat"` to the frozenset) as a reference, and to test a plugin-registration-based fix.

### Note

This was found while shipping a public platform plugin (`hermes-napcat-plugin`); the workaround (local core patch) is in use now, so this is not blocking us — filing for visibility and to fix the design gap for all plugin platforms.

items.title: [Bug]: Upstage solar-pro4 and syn-pro resolve to the 256K default context

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

items.body:
### What happened

`get_model_context_length` returns 256000 for two models in the Upstage chat
catalog when the Upstage provider is selected:

| model | Hermes returns (provider=upstage) | Upstage reports |
|---|---|---|
| `solar-pro4` | 256000 | 524288 |
| `syn-pro` | 256000 | 65536 |

`syn-pro` is the damaging one. Hermes packs the prompt to 4x the real window,
so the request fails at the server instead of compressing in time. `solar-pro4`
loses half of its 512K window.

### Why

Neither id is in `DEFAULT_CONTEXT_LENGTHS` (agent/model_metadata.py), so both
fall through to `DEFAULT_FALLBACK_CONTEXT` at step 8.

The models.dev path cannot cover the gap either: `"upstage"` is absent from
`PROVIDER_TO_MODELS_DEV` (agent/models_dev.py), so `lookup_models_dev_context`
returns None at its first line and step 5g never reads any data. That was
correct when the provider landed in #64541 — models.dev had no Upstage provider
then. It now ships one with `solar-pro4`, `solar-pro3`, `solar-pro2` and
`solar-mini`.

The step-6 OpenRouter fallback does not rescue it, because it is gated on
`not effective_provider` — the resolver skips the community catalog for every
known provider on purpose.

### Reproduce

    python3 -c "
    from agent.model_metadata import get_model_context_length as G
    U = dict(provider='upstage', base_url='https://api.upstage.ai/v1')
    print('solar-pro4', G('solar-pro4', **U))
    print('syn-pro   ', G('syn-pro', **U))"

    solar-pro4 256000
    syn-pro    256000

`provider=` matters. Without it, `solar-pro4` resolves to 524288 through the
step-6 OpenRouter fallback, which indexes the bare alias from
`upstage/solar-pro4`. A configured Upstage user never reaches that step.
`syn-pro` is absent from OpenRouter as well and reads 256000 on either path.

### Source of the correct values

`GET https://api.upstage.ai/v1/solar/models` reports `max_model_len` per id.
The OpenAI-compatible `/v1/models` lists the same chat catalog with no context
field, which is why the resolver cannot read the window from the endpoint:

    solar-pro4-260806   524288   <- absent from DEFAULT_CONTEXT_LENGTHS
    solar-pro3-260323   131072
    solar-pro2-251215    65536
    solar-mini-250422    32768
    syn-pro-251021       65536   <- absent from DEFAULT_CONTEXT_LENGTHS

The three unmarked rows already match the table on main. Same endpoint, same
call — which is why the two marked values can be trusted.

A chat request for the bare `solar-pro4` returns 200 and echoes
`"model": "solar-pro4-260806"`, so the alias and the dated id share one window.
The same holds for `syn-pro` and `syn-pro-251021`.

### Environment

macOS 26.6, Python 3.12, main @ 4a2198bf5124

items.title: [Bug]: Gateway turn-inactivity watchdog abandons turns whose tool call runs silently >30 min

labels.name: sweeper:risk-message-delivery
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may drop, duplicate, misroute, or suppress messages

items.body:
### Bug Description

When a turn's tool call (e.g. `terminal`) runs longer than the gateway turn-inactivity timeout without producing intermediate activity, the watchdog treats the agent as idle and hard-abandons the turn mid-execution, reaping the tool's processes.

`gateway/run.py` `_watch_gateway_turn_inactivity()` polls `agent.get_activity_summary()["seconds_since_activity"]` and calls `_abandon_timed_out_gateway_turn()` (hard interrupt + process reap) once idle >= timeout (default 1800s). Activity is stamped when a tool **starts** (`agent/tool_executor.py` `_touch_activity("executing tool: <name>")`) but is not refreshed while the tool runs unless the tool itself pushes updates. A tool that runs silently for 30+ minutes (quiet builds, long pytest suites, large downloads, network waits) therefore looks idle to the watchdog.

### Evidence (live gateway log)

```
2026-08-03 14:42:18,225 ERROR gateway.run: Agent idle for 1801s (timeout 1800s) in session agent:main:discord:thread:1500021549741244547:1500021549741244547 | last_activity=executing tool: terminal | iteration=57/90 | tool=terminal
```

Note the log itself reports `last_activity=executing tool: terminal`: the system knows a tool is in flight, yet the turn is abandoned anyway.

### Impact

- Legitimate long-running tool calls are killed mid-flight (partial builds, interrupted downloads, orphaned side effects from reaped processes).
- The agent turn is lost with a generic idle-timeout error, which looks like a crash to the user.

### Suggested fix directions

1. Refresh the activity stamp while a tool call is in flight (heartbeat every N seconds while `_current_tool` is set).
2. Exclude in-flight tool execution from the idle window, with a separate (and configurable) hard ceiling for genuinely hung tools.
3. Or expose the turn-inactivity timeout as a gateway config knob so long-tool workloads can raise it.

### Environment

- hermes-agent v0.20.0 gateway (Linux), Python 3.14, Discord platform.

items.title: [Bug]: Prompt caching never engages for LiteLLM on the OpenAI-compatible wire

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

labels.name: sweeper:risk-caching
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may break/degrade prompt caching or cache-key stability (invariant)

items.body:
### Bug Description

`anthropic_prompt_cache_policy()` grants Anthropic `cache_control` markers to a LiteLLM
endpoint only when it is reached over the **native Anthropic wire**
(`api_mode == "anthropic_messages"`).

A LiteLLM deployment that exposes the **OpenAI-compatible** surface instead —
`/v1/chat/completions`, with `/v1/messages` returning 404 — matches no grant branch and
falls through to `(False, False)`. No `cache_control` is injected, the system prompt goes
on the wire as a plain string, and the provider serves **zero cache hits**: _the entire
prompt is re-billed at full price on every turn_.

The endpoint itself supports caching fine. Only the policy's provider detection misses it.

This is the same failure class the function's own docstring already documents for
Qwen/DashScope:

> Without markers these providers serve zero cache hits, re-billing the full prompt on
> every turn.

Impact is significant on long conversations, where the resent transcript dominates input
cost. Because there is no error and no warning, it is silent — usage simply shows 100%
uncached input forever.

There is no configuration workaround: `prompt_caching.cache_ttl` can only *disable*
caching, never force it on.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Point Hermes at a LiteLLM proxy that exposes the OpenAI-compatible API and serves a
   Claude model (`/v1/chat/completions` works; `/v1/messages` returns 404), e.g.
   `provider: custom:litellm`, `model: claude-opus-5`.
2. Evaluate the policy for that configuration:

```python
from types import SimpleNamespace
from agent.agent_runtime_helpers import anthropic_prompt_cache_policy

agent = SimpleNamespace(
    provider="custom:litellm",
    base_url="https://<your-litellm-host>/v1",
    api_mode="chat_completions",
    model="claude-opus-5",
    _cache_disabled=False,
)
print(anthropic_prompt_cache_policy(agent))   # -> (False, False)
```

3. Run any multi-turn session and inspect usage. `cache_read_tokens` and
   `cache_write_tokens` stay at `0` for every call.

**Independent confirmation that the endpoint does support caching** — identical ~5.5k-token
prefix, varying user suffix, streaming with `stream_options={"include_usage": True}`:

```
system as list + cache_control : call 1  create=7007  read=0
                                call 2  create=0     read=7007   <- caching works
system as plain string          : call 1  create=0     read=0
                                call 2  create=0     read=0     <- what Hermes sends today
```

A 10-call run in the first shape held a 100% hit rate against a single backend
deployment, ruling out load-balancer cache-namespace thrash.

> **Note when reproducing:** if your LiteLLM has response caching enabled
> (`litellm_settings.cache: true`), bypass it with `{"cache": {"no-cache": true}}` in the
> request body. Otherwise LiteLLM replays a cached response along with its stored `usage`
> blob, and the numbers you read are not from the provider. The tell is a response
> returning in single-digit milliseconds with an `x-litellm-cache-key` header and no
> `llm_provider-*` headers.

### Expected Behavior

A LiteLLM-fronted Claude model receives `cache_control` markers regardless of whether the
proxy is reached over the Anthropic wire or the OpenAI-compatible wire, and prompt caching
engages — as it already does for OpenRouter, Nous Portal, native Anthropic, and LiteLLM in
Anthropic proxy mode.

### Actual Behavior

`anthropic_prompt_cache_policy()` returns `(False, False)`. No `cache_control` is emitted,
the provider reports `cache_read_input_tokens = 0` and `cache_creation_input_tokens = 0` on
every request, and the full prompt is billed at the uncached rate on every turn. No error
or warning is surfaced.

### Affected Component

Agent Core (conversation loop, context compression, memory)

### Messaging Platform (if gateway-related)

_No response_

### Debug Report

```shell
Left out - the issue should have enough details for reviewing the issue and replicating it.
```

### Operating System

macOS 26.5.2 (Apple Silicon)

### Python Version

3.13.0

### Hermes Version

0.20.0

### Additional Logs / Traceback (optional)

```shell

```

### Root Cause Analysis (optional)

In `agent/agent_runtime_helpers.py::anthropic_prompt_cache_policy()`, the grant branches
cover:

- native Anthropic → `(True, True)`
- OpenRouter / Nous Portal Claude or Kimi → `(True, False)`
- Nous Portal Qwen → `(True, False)`
- `is_anthropic_wire and is_claude` (third-party Anthropic-compatible gateway) → `(True, True)`

LiteLLM is only reachable through the fourth branch, which requires
`api_mode == "anthropic_messages"`. A LiteLLM deployment exposing the OpenAI-compatible
surface has `api_mode == "chat_completions"`, so it matches nothing and falls through to
`(False, False)`.

Two things that look like the cause but are not, ruled out while diagnosing:

1. **Usage parsing.** Hermes handles all three usage shapes correctly, including
   `prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens`, and does send
   `stream_options={"include_usage": True}` on the streaming path. Nothing was being
   dropped — the fields were genuinely zero on the wire.
2. **LiteLLM response caching.** With `litellm_settings.cache: true`, repeat requests are
   served from Redis along with a stale `usage` blob, which makes cache metrics
   unreadable until bypassed. This masks the real behaviour but is not the bug.


### Proposed Fix (optional)

Add one branch after the existing `is_anthropic_wire and is_claude` case:

```python
    # LiteLLM on the OpenAI-compatible wire. The branch above only matches
    # LiteLLM in Anthropic proxy mode; a deployment exposing
    # /v1/chat/completions falls through to (False, False) and serves zero
    # cache hits, re-billing the whole prompt every turn. Same failure class
    # already documented above for Qwen/DashScope.
    _is_litellm_endpoint = (
        "litellm" in eff_provider.strip().lower()
        or "litellm" in base_url_hostname(eff_base_url).lower()
    )
    if _is_litellm_endpoint and is_claude and not is_anthropic_wire:
        return True, True
```

Design notes:

- **Matches on provider string *or* base_url host.** Provider naming varies per install
  (`litellm`, `custom:litellm`, …), so the hostname is the more reliable signal.
- **Gated on the Claude family only.** That is what was empirically verified; a
  Gemini/GPT route through the same proxy must not receive markers.
- **Returns the inner-block layout** `(True, True)`. Both layouts were accepted by the
  endpoint under test; the native form is emitted so the wire shape matches the
  `anthropic_messages` branch for the same gateway.
- **`prompt_caching.cache_ttl: false` still wins** — the early return at the top of the
  function is untouched.

### Measured effect

Same model (`claude-opus-5`) on both sides, real sessions, billing-weighted as
`input×1.0 + cache_read×0.1 + cache_write×1.25`:

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Cache-read share of input-side tokens | 14.3% | 95.9% |
| Input-equivalent units per API call | ~199,000 | ~30,073 |

Independently corroborated by the proxy's own billing dashboard, which showed
per-request cost falling by roughly the same order over the following days.

### Tests

A test file covering the new branch plus guards is ready to include in the PR:

- **Grant:** Claude-family models on a LiteLLM OpenAI-wire endpoint, across several model
  spellings and both provider naming conventions.
- **No over-reach:** non-Claude models on the same proxy get nothing; the
  `prompt_caching.cache_ttl` operator disable still wins; unrelated providers unaffected.
- **Adjacent regression:** native Anthropic still `(True, True)`; OpenRouter Claude still
  `(True, False)` envelope layout; `anthropic_messages` + Claude still `(True, True)`.

Currently 8 fail before the change and 14 pass after. The no-over-reach and
adjacent-regression cases pass both before and after — they pin existing behaviour rather
than the new branch.

### Are you willing to submit a PR for this?

- [x] I'd like to fix this myself and submit a PR

items.title: Update indicator stuck at "1 commit behind" (placeholder) after --depth 1 check breaks merge-base on shallow installer checkouts

labels.name: comp/cli
labels.description: CLI entry point, hermes_cli/, setup wizard

labels.name: needs-decision
labels.description: Awaiting maintainer decision before any implementation

labels.name: sweeper:risk-compatibility
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may break existing users, config, migrations, defaults, or upgrades

items.body:
## Summary

On installer checkouts (which `git clone --depth 1` by design), the update-check paths in the CLI banner and `hermes update --check` fetch with `--depth 1` to stay shallow. That fetch **marks the freshly fetched remote tip as a shallow boundary in `.git/shallow`** — even when the tip's parent commit is already present locally. From that moment `git merge-base HEAD origin/main` fails permanently, and every update indicator (desktop poller, CLI banner, `hermes update --check`) reports a placeholder **"1 commit behind"** instead of the real count, no matter how far `main` has advanced.

The condition is **not self-healing**: the desktop poller's plain `git fetch` is a no-op while the tip is unchanged, and subsequent new tips connect to the boundary commit, so the merge-base never recovers until the repo is unshallowed (`git fetch --unshallow origin main`).

Real-world impact (verified on my machine): the indicator said "1 commit behind" while the checkout was actually **61 commits behind**. Users are misled about how stale their install is, and the same placeholder feeds the desktop "update available" toast.

## Environment

- macOS 26.6.1; installed via the official installer (shallow `git clone --depth 1` of `https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent.git`)
- Backend v0.20.0 (checkout at `936dd73`); desktop shell v0.17.0 (both versions shown in the status bar)
- Affected code paths confirmed **identical on current `main` (`222465d84`)**:
  - `hermes_cli/update_cmd.py:2307` — `depth_args = ["--depth", "1"] if is_shallow else []`
  - `hermes_cli/banner.py:249-250` — `if is_shallow: fetch_args += ["--depth", "1"]`
  - `apps/desktop/electron/update-count.ts` — `resolveBehindCount` returns `1` ("behind by an unknown amount") when `isShallow && !hasMergeBase`

## Steps to reproduce

1. Install via the installer (shallow `clone --depth 1`). Update once, so HEAD becomes the shallow boundary.
2. Wait for upstream `main` to advance; run `hermes update --check`, or start the CLI so the banner prefetch runs. On a shallow repo this fetches with `--depth 1`, writing the new tip into `.git/shallow`.
3. Observe: `git merge-base HEAD origin/main` now exits 1; the desktop/CLI update indicator shows **"1 commit behind"**.
4. Let `main` advance further; the indicator stays at "1 commit behind" — the poller's plain fetch cannot repair the boundary.

Minimal reproduction (verified on a clean setup):

```
# full clone, then a new commit lands on the remote:
git fetch --depth 1 origin main        # tip becomes a shallow boundary
git merge-base HEAD origin/main        # FAILS (exit 1)
git fetch origin main                  # no-op — boundary stays
git merge-base HEAD origin/main        # still FAILS
# a further remote commit + plain fetch: still FAILS (new tip connects to the boundary)
```

## Expected vs. Actual

- **Expected:** the indicator shows the real commit count whenever the history between HEAD and the tip is locally available (the desktop poller's plain fetch provides exactly that).
- **Actual:** after a single `--depth 1` check, the indicator is stuck at the placeholder "1" indefinitely, until `git fetch --unshallow`.

## Root cause

Two mechanisms that were each reasonable in isolation compound on shallow clones:

1. `eecb5b9dd1` (#50784) added the shallow-preserving `--depth 1` fetch to the CLI check paths, to avoid unshallowing the repo and counting a bogus huge number (e.g. "12492 commits behind"). Side effect: git records the freshly fetched tip as a shallow boundary **unconditionally** — even when its parent is already local — which breaks the merge-base between HEAD and origin/main from that moment on.
2. `a6485bddb8` (#52201) added `resolveBehindCount` to the desktop count path, which returns `1` as a presence-only placeholder whenever `isShallow && !hasMergeBase`.

The desktop poller's own fetch (`apps/desktop/electron/main.ts:2559`, `git fetch --quiet origin main` without `--depth`) *can* count correctly — but only as long as no `--depth 1` check has run in between. Once the tip is a boundary, later fetches cannot reach HEAD across it.

## Suggested fix

In the shallow check paths (`update_cmd.py` / `banner.py`), probe whether the new tip's parent is already present locally before choosing `--depth 1`:

```python
if is_shallow:
    # only keep the boundary when the tip's parent is NOT already local;
    # otherwise --depth 1 saves no transfer and only poisons merge-base
    parent_known = subprocess.run(
        git_cmd + ["cat-file", "-e", f"{tip_sha}^"],
        cwd=PROJECT_ROOT, capture_output=True,
    ).returncode == 0
    depth_args = [] if parent_known else ["--depth", "1"]
```

When the parent is already local, `--depth 1` saves nothing (no history would be transferred anyway) and only adds the harmful boundary — a plain scoped fetch keeps the exact-count path and the clone shallow. Alternatively `hermes update` could unshallow once, but that changes the installer's storage trade-off; the probe is the minimal fix.

labels.name: comp/agent

items.body:
## Summary

`execute_tool_calls_sequential` (`agent/tool_executor.py`) executes a single tool call with **no deadline**. Parallel tool batches are bounded by `_DEFAULT_CONCURRENT_TOOL_TIMEOUT_S = 420.0` (line 99, used only in `execute_tool_calls_concurrent`), but the sequential path used for a lone tool call has no equivalent guard — a hung call blocks the whole turn indefinitely until the CLI/gateway process is restarted.

## Impact

Observed on 2026-08-11: a single `web_extract` whose SSE stream lost the tool-result message wedged the session for **21 hours** (02:12 → 23:31, only cleared by the nightly planned gateway restart). The root cause of the hang was a lost SSE message (mcp 1.28.1 client vs mcp 2.x server), fixed client-side, but the executor gap is general: ANY wedged tool on the sequential path can block a turn with no recovery path — no timeout, no interrupt re-entry, no `tool_timeout` disposition like the concurrent path emits at line 1380.

## Evidence (local log mining, 2026-08-05..12)

- 8 parallel-batch timeouts at exactly 420s (bounded, recoverable — loud failure)
- 2 single-call infinite hangs (silent, turn-wedging until restart)
- `execute_tool_calls_sequential` (`agent/tool_executor.py:1603`) contains no timeout/waiter bound; the loop just awaits each tool directly

## Suggested fix

Give the sequential path the same deadline semantics as the concurrent one:

1. Reuse `_resolve_concurrent_tool_timeout()` (or a new config key, e.g. `agent.single_tool_timeout`) as a bound on each sequential tool call.
2. On timeout, emit the same `error_type="tool_timeout"` disposition the concurrent path uses (line 1380) so downstream logic treats it consistently.
3. Consider a bounded future-wait with the same `wait(not_done, timeout)` pattern already used at lines 1249-1255.

Happy to open a PR if the maintainers agree with the approach.

labels.name: comp/agent

labels.description: Sweeper risk: may lose/corrupt/mis-associate session or context state

items.body:
## Summary

`MemoryManager` runs a single worker with an unbounded future set and an unbounded submission queue (`agent/memory_manager.py`). A stuck memory provider makes every turn retain futures, closures and complete transcripts, growing RAM without limit.

## Root cause

- Executor: one worker + set of futures (`agent/memory_manager.py:384-393`).
- `sync_all` captures full messages every turn (`~L638-694`).
- `_submit_background` neither bounds nor coalesces (`~L698-734`).
- A hung provider → unbounded backlog; every queued task pins the full transcript snapshot it captured.

## Impact

- RAM growth to OOM in long gateway sessions when a provider stalls.
- No visibility into backlog depth or oldest-task age.

## Proposed fix

- Bounded queue with drop/coalesce policy (drop duplicate prefetch of the same query; keep latest snapshot per session).
- Minimal per-task snapshot (only what the provider contract needs, not the full transcript).
- Metrics: queue depth, oldest task age, approximate retained bytes, drops/coalesces.
- Durability: spool/coalesce per session or apply backpressure instead of silently discarding.

items.title: [Bug] Commit-time memory callbacks run inside the compaction fence — hung provider can stall the turn

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

labels.name: sweeper:risk-session-state
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may lose/corrupt/mis-associate session or context state

items.body:
## Summary

External callbacks run inside/around the compaction commit fence (`agent/conversation_compression.py`), including a synchronous `commit_memory_session` that can hit network/LLM before the SQLite commit. Four stuck callbacks can saturate the global thread pool and block the fence indefinitely.

## Root cause

- Fence starts at `agent/conversation_compression.py:~L3098-3129`.
- `commit_memory_session` runs inline before SQLite (`~L3251-3255`) and can call network/LLM (`run_agent.py:~L4148-4171`, `agent/memory_manager.py:~L865-875`).
- After the commit starts, timeout waits in slices (`agent/conversation_compression.py:~L819-855`, `~L994-1051`).
- Callbacks blocked in the shared executor starve other fence waiters.

## Impact

- Compaction (and thus the turn) can stall behind a slow/hung memory provider or external hook.
- Global executor starvation: unrelated callbacks queue behind the stuck ones.

## Proposed fix

- Run slow callbacks **outside** the fence; when possible after the durable commit.
- Dedicated bounded executor for commit-time callbacks, with per-callback timeout and a circuit breaker.
- Do not silently drop durable writes — surface failures.

## Cross-references

- #79339 (memory provider sync_turn never called — provider lifecycle class)

items.title: [Bug] Summarizer feasibility reserves no output/reasoning/template budget — aux prompt can exceed its own context

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

labels.name: sweeper:risk-session-state
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may lose/corrupt/mis-associate session or context state

items.body:
## Summary

The summarizer's feasibility check equates the threshold with `aux_context` and reserves nothing for the template, output tokens or reasoning tokens — so an iterative auxiliary prompt can exceed its own context window (e.g. two 160K-char blocks + memory/template into a 64K aux window), and the call performs no fit enforcement.

## Root cause

- Feasibility: threshold == `aux_context`, no reservation (`agent/conversation_compression.py:~L1679-1722`).
- Iterative summarization can sum two ~160K-char blocks + memory/template (`agent/context_compressor.py:~L3823-3853`, `~L4137-4160`) into a 64K aux model.
- No fit enforcement on the outgoing call (`~L4182-4242`).

## Impact

- Aux calls that exceed the model's own context → provider errors, wasted tokens, silent truncation.

## Proposed fix

- Budget = `aux_ctx − output − reasoning − template − memory`; split previous/new dynamically.
- Fit-check before sending (truncate/abort with a clear signal rather than sending an oversized prompt).
- Post-summary size validation (see also the summary-limits issue).

items.title: [Bug] Tool-call argument pruning result is discarded — oversized payload re-sent every turn

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

labels.name: sweeper:risk-session-state
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may lose/corrupt/mis-associate session or context state

items.body:
## Summary

Tool-call argument pruning computes a truncation but discards the result: `_truncate_tool_call_args_at` returns `modified` without incrementing `pruned`, pass 3 ignores its return value, and if nothing else prunes, the function returns the original input — so a large payload is re-sent every turn.

## Root cause

`agent/context_compressor.py`:

- `_truncate_tool_call_args_at` returns `modified` but does not increase `pruned` (`~L3279-3297`).
- Pass 3 ignores the return (`~L3303-3312`).
- Without another prune, the function returns the original input (`~L3454-3463`).

## Impact

- Oversized tool-call arguments survive compression; the full payload is re-sent on every turn and every retry.
- Compression appears ineffective for this class of payload.

## Proposed fix

- Count arg truncation as real pruning (increment the pruned metric).
- Honor the return of `_truncate_tool_call_args_at` in pass 3.
- Ensure the final return reflects the pruned (not the original) arguments.

items.title: [Bug] Tool token-estimate cache keyed by id(list) returns stale estimates (middle mutations invisible)

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

labels.name: sweeper:risk-session-state
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may lose/corrupt/mis-associate session or context state

items.body:
## Summary

The tool-schema token-estimate cache (`_TOOLS_TOKENS_CACHE`) is keyed by `id(list)` and validates only size + first/last tool name. Mutations to tools in the middle of the list are invisible to the cache, and `id()` values can be recycled after GC — producing stale estimates that drive compression too early or too late.

## Root cause

`agent/model_metadata.py`:

- `_estimate_tools_tokens_rough` keys on `id(tools)` (`~L3322-3331`).
- Cache entry stores `(n, first_name, last_name, tokens)`; a description change to any middle tool is never detected.
- Synthetic repro: before = `6`; after growing a middle description the cache still returned `6`; recompute = `10.006`.

## Impact

- Stale token estimates: premature or late compression, wrong preflight numbers.
- Recycled `id()` can return a wrong cached estimate for an unrelated list.

## Proposed fix

- Use a stable digest/version of the schemas (e.g. hash of names+descriptions+parameters, or a generation counter bumped on toolset rebuild) instead of `id(list)`.
- Keep a strong reference or use a generation-based key so recycled ids can't alias.

## Cross-references

- #8039 (cache correctness in model_metadata.py)

items.title: [Bug] Prompt-cache TTL regresses to 5m in MoA/aux, Qwen 1h marker unclamped, failover skips re-preflight

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

labels.name: P0
labels.description: Critical — data loss, security, crash loop

labels.name: sweeper:risk-caching
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may break/degrade prompt caching or cache-key stability (invariant)

items.body:
## Summary

Prompt-cache TTL and stable-prefix handling degrade in auxiliary/MoA paths, and a Qwen-specific clamp is missing:

1. The main loop propagates `agent._cache_ttl` and the stable prefix (`agent/conversation_loop.py:~L2110-2124`), but the MoA/aux helper only accepts `cache_disabled` (`agent/agent_runtime_helpers.py:~L2009-2065`); MoA passes only that field (`agent/moa_loop.py:~L1738-1754`). Result: `1h` regresses to `5m` and MoA marks the whole system prompt as a breakpoint.
2. `_build_marker` always accepts `ttl:'1h'` (`agent/prompt_caching.py:~L115-120`) with no capability clamp — Qwen/Alibaba documents an explicit context cache of **five minutes** (renewed on hit), so `1h` is ignored/rejected and the expectation of a hit is false.
3. After failover to a smaller context window the compressor gets the new limit (`agent/chat_completion_helpers.py:~L2351-2378`), but the preflight is not repeated before the retry (`agent/conversation_loop.py:~L2478-2507`) — the first fallback call is still knowingly oversized.

## Impact

- More cache writes/misses and cost on MoA/aux flows.
- False 1h-cache expectations on Qwen (field ignored/rejected).
- One oversized request per provider/model failover, before any compression happens.

## Proposed fix

- Capability matrix per transport/provider/route/model with an effective TTL; propagate TTL + static prefix through the MoA/aux helper.
- Clamp Qwen to 5m (or drop the marker) until a 1h capability is proven.
- Re-run preflight after any context-window/model/provider change, before the first network call.

## Cross-references

- #79012/#79013/#79017 (prompt_cache_key scope propagation class)
- #14971 (closed: configurable prompt cache TTL)
- Docs: Anthropic 5m/1h; OpenRouter writes 5m@1.25x / 1h@2x, reads 0.1x; Qwen Alibaba context cache 5m.

items.title: [Bug] Gateway memory-pressure sweep runs only on the 300s watcher; auto targets 65% of total RAM
items.body:
## Summary

Gateway agent-cache pressure is checked only on the 300s watcher tick, and `auto` targets 65% of total RAM — so a burst of large transcripts can OOM the process before the next sweep, and on a 64GiB host the threshold is ~41.6 GiB.

## Root cause

- `gateway/agent_cache_pressure.py:~L1-21` acknowledges 128 transcripts can occupy several GiB; `auto` uses 65% of cgroup or total RAM (`~L35-43`, `~L156-182`).
- The pressure sweep only runs on the default 300s watcher (`gateway/run.py:~L12286-12295`, `~L12419-12442`).
- Soft eviction guards are good (`gateway/run.py:~L24415-24579`), but the token-memo cache still pins raw strings (see the RAM issue).

## Impact

- Process OOM / swap thrash on bursty multi-session gateways before any eviction runs.
- Very high effective threshold on big hosts.

## Proposed fix

- Run a pressure check after each turn and after each cache insertion, plus a short sampler.
- Budget from available memory + a configurable absolute RSS cap (not only a percentage of total).
- Keep the eviction guards; add metrics (RSS, est. bytes per transcript, eviction count).

## Cross-references

- #84710 (tool concurrency counts calls, not weight/RSS — same pressure class)

items.title: [Bug] Persistent context cache does read-modify-write without lock, atomic replace or TTL

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

labels.name: sweeper:risk-compatibility
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may break existing users, config, migrations, defaults, or upgrades

items.body:
## Summary

The persistent context-window cache (`agent/model_metadata.py`) does read-modify-write with `open(..., 'w')` — no lock, no atomic replace, no TTL, no version. Concurrent writers can lose updates or corrupt the file, and the key (`model@base_url`) has no timestamp or account, so a stale value can win indefinitely.

## Root cause

`agent/model_metadata.py:~L1411-1507`:

- `open(..., 'w')` truncate-write without a lock or `os.replace`.
- Key contains `model@base_url` only (`~L1431-1438`) — no timestamp/account.
- No TTL on read-back.

## Impact

- Lost updates under concurrent metadata fetches (gateway multiplex).
- Corrupt/partial JSON on crash mid-write.
- Stale context limit served indefinitely after a provider change.

## Proposed fix

- Atomic write via tempfile + `os.replace`; serialize writers with a lock or CAS.
- Add TTL, version field, and account/scope in the key.
- Prefer last-known-good semantics (see the Portal LKG issue).

items.title: [Bug] 10K summary limit is advisory; micro max_tokens consumed by reasoning — cursor advances, content skipped

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

labels.name: sweeper:risk-session-state
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may lose/corrupt/mis-associate session or context state

items.body:
## Summary

The 10K summary limit is advisory-only (an instruction, not enforced), and micro-compaction uses a hard `max_tokens` cap that can be consumed entirely by reasoning tokens on reasoning models — three failures advance the cursor, skipping the content permanently.

## Root cause

- Summary 10K is just an instruction (`agent/context_compressor.py:~L487-494`, `~L4193-4201`, `~L4243-4296`).
- Micro uses a rigid `max_tokens` (`~L5873-5911`) with no reasoning reservation; on reasoning models the budget can vanish into reasoning output.
- Three failures advance the cursor (`~L6072-6100`) — content is skipped, not retried.

## Impact

- Over-long summaries (cost, cache pollution).
- Reasoning models: truncated/empty summaries or permanent skip of compressible content.

## Proposed fix

- Post-response summary size validation (reject/retry oversize).
- Reserve reasoning tokens in the micro budget; align the cap with reasoning-model behavior.
- Do not advance the cursor on failure without a durable reason and a retry path.

items.title: [Bug] Compacted snapshots and FTS have no quota/retention — unbounded disk and degraded search

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

labels.name: sweeper:risk-session-state
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may lose/corrupt/mis-associate session or context state

items.body:
## Summary

Compacted snapshots and FTS entries have no quota or retention: every compaction archives raw turns/snapshots and FTS keeps indexing compacted material, so long sessions degrade disk usage, checkpoint cost and search quality without bound.

## Root cause

- Each compaction archives raw turns/snapshots (`hermes_state.py:~L8287-8359`).
- FTS continues searching compacted material (`hermes_state_search.py:~L1371-1372`, `~L1559-1560`, `~L1788-1795`).

## Impact

- Unbounded disk growth per session; slower checkpoints and searches.
- Search results dominated by stale compacted copies of the same content.

## Proposed fix

- Per-session quota with cold archive (move, don't destroy — keep recoverability).
- Retention policy for archived snapshots.
- FTS: exclude or de-prioritize compacted/archived material, or rebuild indexes after compaction.

items.title: [Bug] Retry-After: HTTP-date values ignored, negative values not clamped to 0

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

items.body:
## Summary

The main loop reimplements `Retry-After` parsing and mishandles two cases: HTTP-date values are ignored (falls back to generic jitter), and negative numeric values are not clamped to 0 — `min(float(x), 600)` only bounds the top.

## Root cause

`agent/conversation_loop.py:~L5897-5912`:

```python
_ra_raw = _resp_headers.get("retry-after") or _resp_headers.get("Retry-After")
if _ra_raw:
    try:
        _retry_after = min(float(_ra_raw), 600)
    except (TypeError, ValueError):
        pass
```

- `"Wed, 21 Oct 2015 07:28:00 GMT"` → `ValueError` → header ignored (HTTP-date per RFC 9110).
- `"-5"` → `min(-5, 600)` = `-5` → `wait_time = -5` → invalid/negative sleep (or immediate retry).

## Impact

- Retry earlier than the provider asked (HTTP-date), re-tripping the limit.
- Negative wait can crash the sleep or retry instantly.

## Proposed fix

- Parse both delta-seconds and HTTP-date (email.utils.parsedate_to_datetime).
- Clamp to `[0, 600]` (or a sane minimum like 0.5s).
- Keep the existing 600s cap and the jittered-backoff fallback for missing headers.

items.title: [Bug] Tool-schema caches are FIFO not LRU; Nous account cache is single-slot thrash

labels.name: comp/portal
labels.description: Nous portal / Hermes Pro / hosted-Hermes path

items.body:
## Summary

The tool-schema caches behave as FIFO, not LRU: the outer `get_tool_definitions()` memo never reorders on hit, and the Nous account cache holds a single slot — a hot key can be evicted and multi-profile multiplexing thrashes.

## Root cause

- Outer tool-definition memo (`model_tools.py:~L276-367`): insertion-ordered; a hit does not move the key to the end, so a hot key can be evicted by one-time builds (relates to CP-07).
- `hermes_cli/nous_account.py:~L399-443`: single-slot account cache → A/B thrash between profiles/accounts.

## Impact

- Rebuild cost (24.4ms vs 42.8µs hit) paid for the hot toolset while cold entries linger.
- Nous account state flapping between identities.

## Proposed fix

- Move-to-end on hit (real LRU) for the outer tool cache; use an OrderedDict touch.
- Multi-slot (or keyed) account cache with scope (see the Nous state issue).

items.title: [Bug] Nous detection by URL substring applies quirks to incompatible hosts

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

items.body:
## Summary

Nous detection is done by URL substring, so provider-specific quirks and cache markers get applied to incompatible hosts/paths, and non-Nous routes can miss Nous-specific behavior.

## Root cause

- Nous-ness derived from substring matching on the base URL rather than the resolved route/model capability (see CP-14/15/16 for the same class on cache capability).
- Substring matches are fragile: a proxy path or a custom domain containing the substring inherits Nous quirks; a Nous route behind a custom endpoint can be missed.

## Impact

- Wrong markers/behaviors on unrelated providers.
- Missed Nous-specific handling on legitimately-proxied routes.

## Proposed fix

- Route/model-based capability resolution (transport + provider id + host match + route), not substring family checks.
- Centralize the detection so one matrix serves cache capability, rate-guard and account logic.

## Cross-references

- #84707 (Gemma inherits Gemini thought_signature replay via substring match — same defect class)

labels.name: needs-decision
labels.description: Awaiting maintainer decision before any implementation

labels.name: sweeper:risk-security-boundary
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may affect sandboxing, auth, credentials, or sensitive data

labels.name: comp/dashboard
labels.description: Web dashboard / control panel UI (dashboard/, landing)

items.body:
## Summary

Dashboard authentication is not authorization: any identity that passes signature/issuer/audience validation becomes a session with host-owner authority. There is no subject/group/domain allowlist, no RBAC, no per-user session ownership, and the file-session API can operate without a locked root. The real contract today is **single-owner dashboard**, not multi-tenant.

## Root cause

- Self-hosted OIDC: validates signature/issuer/audience/claims (`plugins/dashboard_auth/self_hosted/__init__.py:~L625-633`) and creates a session for any valid identity (`~L678-710`). No subject/group/domain allowlist.
- Nous provider: validates RS256/aud/issuer/instance (`plugins/dashboard_auth/nous/__init__.py:~L430-499`) and maps org (`~L517-537`); middleware auto-approves any org member (`hermes_cli/dashboard_auth/middleware.py:~L166-191`).
- Session routes do not filter by `session.user_id` (`hermes_cli/web_routers/sessions.py:~L53-159`, `~L555-652`).
- FS API can operate without a locked root (`hermes_cli/web_server.py:~L1929-1946`, `~L2179-2233`, `~L2627-2735`).

## Impact

- In a multi-user IdP deployment, every accepted identity gets host-owner power: full FS, sessions, console.
- Session cross-visibility between users.

## Proposed fix

- Declare and enforce single-owner, OR implement default-deny subject/group policy, RBAC admin/user, per-user session ownership, and a restricted FS root for non-admins.

## Cross-references

- #62549 (Session.user_id never reaches agent construction — multi-user isolation half)

## Summary

The OIDC revocation endpoint receives no validation equivalent to the main token path, and remote binds reduce cookie security. An operator or remote configuration can leave revocation unauthenticated or misconfigured.

## Root cause

- Session revocation can be forged/disabled if the endpoint is reachable.

- Validate the revocation endpoint with the same issuer/auth/token/JWKS policy; disable redirects.
- Require TLS for remote binds unless an explicitly dangerous override is set.

labels.name: dependencies

labels.name: python:uv
labels.description: Pull requests that update python:uv code

labels.name: needs-decision

## Summary

No audited lock file gates security-critical Python dependencies: `pyproject.toml` still pins ranges (not hashes), and the release pipeline has no enforced SBOM + OSV scan. The Python scanner was inconclusive locally (OSV blocked), so a zero-CVE claim for Python is not established.

## Root cause

- `pyproject.toml:~L84`, `~L114-126`, `~L163` use version ranges on security-critical deps.
- `npm audit` is green (1.370 deps, 0 vulns across root/web/ui-tui), but there is no equivalent Python gate.
- Local OSV query failed with connection refused; pip-audit/Bandit/Semgrep/Gitleaks/TruffleHog not installed in the audit environment.

## Impact

- Supply-chain risk (the class behind the litellm compromise and the Mini Shai-Hulud campaign) not continuously scanned for Python.
- Releases can ship a dependency with a known CVE unknowingly.

## Proposed fix

- CI: install as end-user, generate an SBOM, and query OSV before release; fail on known vulnerabilities.
- Consider hash-pinned lock for runtime installs (policy already pins upper bounds; a lock adds integrity).
- Document the audit commands in the release checklist.

## Bug description

Grok 4.6 added a model-specific reasoning ceiling and xAI added Priority Processing to the Responses API, but current `main` still applies two older provider-wide compatibility rules:

1. `agent/transports/codex.py` clamps every xAI Responses `xhigh` effort to `high`.
2. The same transport strips `service_tier` from every xAI Responses request.

That behavior remains correct for Grok 4.5 and earlier models, but is wrong for Grok 4.6. The result is silent loss of the requested reasoning effort and no way to select xAI's priority/fast processing from Hermes.

I checked current `main` at `1d3d021282098261ce2ad224a76d97d89b16188c`, not only a released install. The blanket clamp and strip are still present.

Related work:

- #84661 merged the 500K context entry and reasoning-effort capability allowlist.
- #84341 covers the stale context cache and native xAI model-list fallback.
- #42330 introduced the older provider-wide `xhigh -> high` behavior when Grok did not support `xhigh`.
- #28490 introduced the provider-wide `service_tier` strip when xAI Responses rejected the field.

Neither #84661 nor #84341 changes the transport behavior described here.

## Steps to reproduce

Using Hermes' `ResponsesApiTransport.build_kwargs` on the xAI Responses path:

```python
transport.build_kwargs(
    model="grok-4.6",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "..."}],
    tools=[],
    is_xai_responses=True,
    reasoning_config={"effort": "xhigh"},
    request_overrides={"service_tier": "priority"},
)
```

On current `main`, the resulting request has `reasoning.effort=high`, and `service_tier` is absent.

Also, `hermes_cli.models.model_supports_fast_mode("grok-4.6")` is false, so the `/fast` control cannot generate the otherwise-valid priority override for this model.

## Live probe receipts

These calls were made through a locally model-gated Hermes transport, with no direct request-body bypass.

### Reasoning effort is observable in usage

Same model and prompt, API-key route:

**Low** — HTTP 200, served model `grok-4.6`:

```json
{
  "input_tokens": 364,
  "input_tokens_details": {"cached_tokens": 128},
  "output_tokens": 401,
  "output_tokens_details": {"reasoning_tokens": 362},
  "total_tokens": 765
}
```

**xhigh** — HTTP 200, served model `grok-4.6`:

```json
{
  "input_tokens": 365,
  "input_tokens_details": {"cached_tokens": 128},
  "output_tokens": 1800,
  "output_tokens_details": {"reasoning_tokens": 1767},
  "total_tokens": 2165
}
```

Reasoning-token delta: `1767 - 362 = 1405` on the same prompt. This is an observable confirmation that Grok 4.6 accepts and honors `xhigh` rather than requiring the older clamp.

Negative effort control: `reasoning.effort="definitely-invalid"` survived Hermes and returned HTTP 400, `Invalid reasoning effort.` It was not silently removed.

### Priority Processing survives and is echoed

Requesting `service_tier="priority"` through the same Hermes transport:

| Auth route | HTTP | Served model | Request tier | Response tier |
|---|---:|---|---|---|
| xAI API key | 200 | `grok-4.6` | `priority` | `priority` |
| xAI OAuth | 200 | `grok-4.6` | `priority` | `priority` |

This matches xAI's documented contract that the response echoes the tier actually used.

### There is no separate fast model slug

`model="grok-4.6-fast"` returned HTTP 400, `Model not found: grok-4.6-fast`, on both the API-key and OAuth routes. Fast/priority processing is the `service_tier="priority"` request field, not a separate model ID.

### Grok 4.5 compatibility control

With Hermes configured for `xhigh`, the model-gated transport still sent `reasoning.effort="high"` to `grok-4.5`. The request returned HTTP 200 and served model `grok-4.5`. Earlier Grok behavior is unchanged.

## Expected behavior

- Preserve `xhigh` only for the Grok 4.6 family.
- Continue clamping `xhigh`, `max`, and `ultra` to `high` for Grok 4.5 and other xAI Responses models that do not accept those wire values.
- Preserve `service_tier="priority"` only for the Grok 4.6 family; keep the defensive strip for older xAI models.
- Expose `/fast` for Grok 4.6 and resolve it to `{"service_tier": "priority"}`.
- Keep `max` and `ultra` as Hermes-level aliases only; neither is a valid Grok wire value.

A surgical implementation can model-gate both transport rules by normalized model ID and add bidirectional regression tests for Grok 4.6 versus Grok 4.5.

## Actual behavior

- Grok 4.6 `xhigh` is silently rewritten to `high`.
- Grok 4.6 `service_tier="priority"` is silently removed.
- The CLI fast-mode registry reports Grok 4.6 as unsupported.

## Environment

- Hermes Agent v0.20.0, plus confirmation against current `main` SHA above
- Python 3.11.15
- macOS
- A focused local regression selection passes after model-gating the behavior: 168 tests passed

## Official references

- Grok reasoning effort: https://docs.x.ai/developers/model-capabilities/text/reasoning
- Priority Processing: https://docs.x.ai/developers/advanced-api-usage/priority-processing
- Grok 4.6 model card and 500K context: https://docs.x.ai/developers/models/grok-4.6
- Pricing and long-context threshold: https://docs.x.ai/developers/pricing

## Summary

Opening the Hermes desktop app kills the user's healthy, detached messaging gateway (started as an independent background process via the documented Windows Scheduled Task mechanism), taking Discord and the kanban dispatcher offline. It exits via SIGKILL with no clean shutdown.

The root cause is an intent/implementation mismatch in `_reap_unsupervised_gateway_orphans()`: the function's docstring says it kills orphans *"the pidfile/runtime record can't see,"* but it feeds `find_gateway_pids()` (which **includes** the registered running gateway via `get_running_pid()`) into a SIGTERM→SIGKILL loop — so it kills a healthy, fully-registered gateway that the pidfile CAN see.

## Environment

- OS: Windows 10
- Setup: `hermes gateway install` creates a **Scheduled Task** (`Hermes_Gateway`) that starts the gateway detached at boot (`wscript.exe` → `hermes gateway run`). This is the documented intended design — the desktop app runs `hermes serve` (UI backend) and the messaging gateway is a *separate, independently-started process* (per `website/docs/user-guide/desktop.md`: "the gateway is a separate long-running process you start independently").
- Profiles: multiple (default + ops etc.). `ops` survives; `default` is killed.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Start the default messaging gateway detached (e.g. via the `Hermes_Gateway` Scheduled Task, or `hermes gateway run`).
2. Confirm it's healthy: `hermes gateway list` shows `default` running; Discord connected; kanban dispatcher holds the lock.
3. Launch the Hermes desktop app (`hermes desktop`).

## Expected Behavior

The detached gateway should keep running. Per the docs, the desktop app (`hermes serve`) is a separate frontend and does not own or replace the messaging gateway.

## Actual Behavior

Within ~16s of app launch, the default gateway is killed with **SIGKILL** — `gateway-exit-diag.log` shows *"exited UNCLEANLY (no exit path ran — SIGKILL)"*, no clean exit entry, and `gateway.log` just stops. `ops` (a different profile) survives. Discord disconnects and the kanban dispatcher stops until the gateway is manually restarted.

Observed twice; fully reproducible by relaunching the app.

## Root Cause

`hermes_cli/gateway.py` → `_reap_unsupervised_gateway_orphans()` (~L1528), called at desktop `serve` boot (`web_server.py` ~L241, gated on `HERMES_DESKTOP=1`).

- **Docstring intent:** "Kill no-supervisor gateway orphans the pidfile/runtime record can't see."
- **Implementation bug:** `orphans = [p for p in find_gateway_pids(exclude_pids=own) if p and p > 0]`. `find_gateway_pids()` **includes** the registered running gateway via `get_running_pid()` (gateway.py ~L629-631). So a healthy gateway with a valid `gateway.pid`, active lock, and live process is treated as an orphan and SIGKILLed.
- The desktop app never forks its own messaging gateway (it runs `hermes serve`, a UI backend), so on this boot path the reap clears the way for nothing — it only destroys a healthy independently-managed gateway.

`ops` survives because the reap is `HERMES_HOME`-scoped to the current profile (`default`), so it only matches gateways advertising the current profile.

## Proposed Fix (local, verified working)

In `_reap_unsupervised_gateway_orphans()`, add the currently-registered running gateway PID (`get_running_pid()`) to the exclusion set alongside `os.getpid()` and `extra_exclude`, so the reap only kills gateways the pidfile/runtime record cannot see — matching the documented intent.

- Do NOT change the restart/stop paths (`stop_profile_gateway`, `_spawn_gateway_restart`) — there, killing the registered gateway is intentional and `stop_profile_gateway` already passes `extra_exclude={pid}`.
- Fix at the function level covers both the desktop-boot call and the `_spawn_gateway_restart` call, with no `web_server.py` change.

A local patch implementing this (and a regression test asserting a registered PID is excluded) is in place in a fork and works: `tests/hermes_cli/test_spawn_gateway_restart_reap.py` + `tests/hermes_cli/test_gateway.py` → 13 passed, 5 skipped.

## Notes

- I'm happy to open a PR with the fix if that's preferred; let me know.
- The documented split-brain concern (a newly-forked gateway racing the same credential) is preserved: the fix only stops the reap from killing a gateway the runtime record can see; genuinely unregistered orphans are still reaped.
